articles.title: Somerset woman pregnant years after life-saving transplant
articles.summary: Keeleigh John says her pregnancy would not be possible without her childhood organ donor.
articles.body:
A woman who received a double organ transplant as a child says becoming pregnant would not have been possible without the family of her donor.

Keeleigh John, from Bridgwater in Somerset, was diagnosed with chronic renal failure and underwent life-saving surgery to receive a new liver and kidneys when she was 12 years old.

Keeleigh, now 28, said doctors had told her family it was unlikely she would ever have children.

After recovering from four bouts of sepsis this year, she discovered she was pregnant on the day she returned home from hospital. Keeleigh said she "owes it all" to the donor family who made a decision at probably "the most difficult time in their life".

"We're at the 14-week point now. Baby looks healthy, I'm doing really well," she said.

"They've done all the tests and they've said it's almost impossible for any sort of condition that I have to transfer over to baby."

Keeleigh's mother, Tracy John, said doctors had warned the family that her daughter was unlikely to have children.

"Me and my husband were told years ago we'd be lucky to see her survive to eight, and then it was to 12.

"Then she received a transplant and now she's flying all over the world and having her own children. It's just something we never dreamed of."

Keeleigh now campaigns for organ donation and has competed in the British Transplant Games and international events, winning gold medals in events including shot put, archery and discus.

She is due to find out this week whether she has been selected for the 2027 World Transplant Games in Belgium.

"I'm hoping I'll be on that plane to Belgium next year, hopefully with a tiny little baby."

She said she hoped her achievements would make both her family and her donor's family proud.

Keeleigh actively advocates for the NHS Organ Donor Register, saying: "If you are prepared to accept an organ, you should be prepared to donate one."

Recently, the NHS launched its first "urgent response plan" to address the drop in the number of organs being donated .

NHS Blood and Transplant figures show deceased donation rates are 9% lower than at the same point last year, while the UK transplant waiting list has reached a record high.

Keeleigh said the life she has now, including her pregnancy, was only possible because her donor's family agreed to donation at a difficult time.

"Not only would my life not have been possible, but also now I'm creating a life which also wouldn't have been possible. We never thought it would be possible."

Her mother said the family remained grateful to the donor.

"Without the donor family, for one, I wouldn't have my baby here, and she wouldn't have had the chance to have her own baby," she said.

articles.title: Is Angelina Jolie's handwriting hard to read, or are we out of practice?
articles.summary: A thank-you note written by the actor has turned into something of a modern-day reading challenge.
articles.body:
Can you read Angelina Jolie's handwriting? That's what the internet has been asking this week after a thank-you note the actor wrote in 2023 resurfaced.

Jolie addressed the letter to the staff at a luxury resort in Greece , where she reportedly stayed while filming Maria , the 2024 Maria Callas biopic. Millions of people have viewed the viral note , with many puzzling over what her cryptic script actually says.

While some have argued that Jolie's handwriting is difficult to decipher "even if you read cursive," others have wondered whether the reaction says more about our changing relationship with handwriting than simply her penmanship. "Gen Z needs to learn to read cursive so they can read Angelina Jolie's notes!" one commentator said.

Other celebrities' handwriting has provoked similarly strong reactions, though for different reasons. Jacob Elordi fans were surprised to see the actor's handwriting in a promotional video for last year's Academy Awards . Some commenters said the writing looked like "someone who holds a pencil like a child drawing with a crayon," while others said it was a joke, as he had responded to the Academy's writing prompt with "be funny, when you can."

For many millennials and members of Gen X, learning to write in cursive was a part of growing up. But as keyboards and screens increasingly replace pen and paper, our relationship with handwriting is changing. So are we simply getting out of practice, or are handwriting skills at risk of disappearing altogether?

Cursive became a fixture of American classrooms in the mid-1800s , with children typically learning to write in print first, then learning to connect their letters around the third grade, allowing for "quicker writing with fewer pauses," according to EBSCO's Research Starters . Rules on good penmanship turned handwriting into a disciplined skill. By the early 20th century, there were strict instructions on how to write, with students taught through specific methods to copy uniform letters with rhythmic motion and left-handers required to use their right hands, according to the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History .

Technology then began to change the classroom. Typewriters started appearing in schools in the 1930s and computers followed in the late 1980s, the Smithsonian said, with educators adding typing and keyboarding alongside handwriting. By 2010, cursive was falling out of favor. The Common Core State Standards, which set academic benchmarks for K-12 students, did not require schools to teach cursive. Instead, they emphasized keyboarding skills for students in third through fifth grade.

That shift may help explain the reaction to Jolie's note. Shawn Datchuk, a professor of special education at the University of Iowa College of Education, said he was not surprised that it appeared to divide readers by age.

"With the rise of computer technology over the past decade, many K-12 students are only briefly exposed to cursive handwriting, if at all," Datchuk told Yahoo. Because cursive letters can look drastically different from their printed counterparts, he said, people who haven't learned to read or write them may struggle to understand handwritten notes or historical documents.

The apparent generational divide may therefore have less to do with young people's abilities and more about what they were taught, according to Zoe R. Smith, a psychologist at the University of Denver who has spoken publicly about handwriting vs. typing in education.

Smith, a millennial herself, learned both cursive and typing in elementary school, but only typing continued after sixth grade. "A joke among many millennials is that we were told that we would need cursive for the next educational milestone and never did," she told Yahoo.

Even so, Smith said she could read only about half of Jolie's note, working out the rest from context clues.

Cursive, however, has made something of a comeback in recent years, with some lawmakers and parents concerned that children are missing out on a valuable skill. Republican Indiana state Sen. Jean Leising, for example, has spent more than a decade trying to pass a state law requiring schools to teach it.

Leising argued in a 2018 press release that omitting cursive from the Common Core had left some teenagers unable to sign their names on documents and driver's licenses. She also said there is now a "huge disparity" between public and private school students, pointing to a state survey in which 91% of private schools that responded teach cursive, compared with 52% of public schools.

Now, more than 20 states have passed laws requiring public schools to make time to teach cursive. North Carolina was among the first, with a 2013 law requiring students to write legible cursive by the end of fifth grade. New Jersey's law, signed in January , requires all public school districts to teach cursive reading and writing in grades three through five, starting this school year.

Mary Jean Tecce DeCarlo, a clinical professor of literacy studies at Drexel University, said that while there might be a renewed interest in cursive, reintroducing it could prove challenging. In an essay for the Conversation , she noted that many of today's teachers, and many of tomorrow's, never learned cursive themselves. Teaching it properly can also take roughly 70 minutes a week , she wrote, raising the question of how to fit it into busy school days.

DeCarlo also argues the science is "shakier than cursive's champions let on." There is solid evidence that handwriting beats typing for learning and memory, she wrote, but whether cursive specifically has an edge over ordinary print is much less clear.

That is where Smith lands too. She cautions that bringing cursive back into the curriculum could result in another skill being shelved. "Any time we prioritize something it typically means we should ask, what is being de-prioritized," she said.

For her, the key issue isn't cursive vs. print. "It does not matter if a student is learning cursive or print writing, what matters is that they are learning how to handwrite," she said, arguing that writing by hand helps people learn and remember at every age because it uses motor skills alongside memory.

Whether handwriting is legible may depend as much on the reader as the writer, Datchuk said. While people broadly agree on how letters should look, there is a large range in what they find acceptable. "What appears readable for some people can be unreadable for others," he said. Practice matters, he added, but so do motivation and audience: people tend to write more carefully when a message matters to a loved one, and less legibly when pressed for time.

So is the decline of cursive — and our ability to read it — something to worry about? Datchuk sees three reasons learning cursive may be important. For one, fluent handwriting can help students become better writers and learn advanced writing skills more easily. It may also help reduce screen time in schools, a growing concern for educators and parents.

The third reason, he said, is social. Because the cursive alphabet looks so different from print, children who aren't taught it would struggle to read foundational texts or the handwriting of loved ones, "such as grandmothers or other authors." Ultimately, he said, whether students learn it "is likely influenced by the value (or lack of value) we place on it."

It seems that whether Jolie's handwriting is hard to read may depend less on her penmanship than on who is reading it.

articles.title: Muslim youths set up BJP office in Nandigram after CM Suvendu Adhikari's ‘friendship’ appeal
articles.summary: Muslim youths in Nandigram set up a temporary BJP office after CM Suvendu Adhikari’s “friendship” appeal ahead of Oct 6 bypolls; Congress also campaigns.
articles.body: NANDIGRAM: A day after CM Suvendu Adhikari urged minority voters to build a “friendship” with BJP ahead of the Oct 6 bypolls, local Muslim youths set up a temporary party office in Sarberia using bamboo, tarpaulin and cloth.The office displays portraits of Adhikari and BJP candidate Hasirani Rath.Addressing voters on Saturday, Adhikari said the bypolls in Nandigram and minority-dominated Rejinagar offered minority voters an opportunity to support BJP.“Will our minority brothers and sisters keep turning their faces away from us? Oct 6 is an auspicious day to build a friendship. Prime Minister Narendra Modi works for everyone, and the CM will also work for everyone,” he said, calling polling day “Friendship Day” and promising development.The office was built and inaugurated by members of the minority community in Sarberia village, under the Kendamari area. Local netas said it was the first BJP constituency office in Nandigram established directly by minority supporters.Sanowar Ali Saha, who manages the office, said local Muslim youths had set up the unit following Adhikari’s appeal on Friday to minority voters to “befriend” the BJP and join its development initiatives.Saha, an independent panchayat election winner and former Trinamool worker, said residents were backing BJP voluntarily in support of Adhikari’s development agenda.Sarberia, a battleground during the 2007 anti-land acquisition movement and a traditional Trinamool stronghold, has around 1,700 voters, 70% of whom belong to the minority community. articles.title: Ex-City trader How to spot a psychopath at work
articles.summary: Geraint Anderson says some modern workplaces reward psychopathic traits.
articles.body:
Most of us have had colleagues who can be tricky to work with.

They may act impulsively, be manipulative, or even outright lie to advance their careers - but how can you tell the difference between an unpleasant co-worker and someone displaying psychopathic traits?

Geraint Anderson, a former London banker-turned author, said he was assessed by a clinical psychologist who told him he may have had "situational psychopathy" in order to succeed in the cut-throat corporate world.

"I had to really become a kind of worse version of myself in order to thrive in this environment," he said.

Anderson, 53, who now lives in Monmouthshire, said some modern workplaces and social influences reward psychopathic traits.

He worked for 12 years as an analyst in London's financial district and earned millions of pounds before leaving his job ahead of the financial crash in 2008.

"The city rewards this dark triad behaviour... being uber confident, being able to control and manipulate others, not getting emotionally involved in decisions and being decisive," he said.

"I adapted myself for the city and started bringing out the kind of worst side of myself."

A psychopath is someone with an antisocial personality disorder , rather than a clinical diagnosis itself.

People with these disorders think and act differently to others and, among other things:

Have difficulty sustaining long-term relationships

Lack guilt and blame others for problems in their lives

In his early 20s, Anderson was enjoying life in Goa, India, selling trinkets to tourists on the beach.

His brother convinced him to apply for a finance job, which he only intended to do for a few years.

"I cut off my ponytail, shaved off my beard, took all my earrings out, bought a £60 suit - all that's totally true - the day before I had my interview."

Once he had his foot in the door as an intern, success became an obsession, with bonuses becoming "a way of gauging how wonderfully successful a human being I was".

This figure allowed him to compare himself to people at other banks and "really appealed to my competitiveness".

He believes some of the traits that helped him climb the ranks were those associated with psychopathy.

"I had a degree of fearlessness. I had a bit of - dare I say - glib charm. I wasn't hugely emotionally affected by things that happened on the trading floor."

Anderson said a lot of traits psychopaths possess are ones "that the corporate environment rewards" and are "incredibly useful in high-powered jobs in the city".

He added the most important thing when it comes to psychopaths is "you don't promote them, you don't marry them and you don't vote for them."

Robert Snowden, a Cardiff University psychologist, has studied psychopathy for about 25 years and has worked with Robert Hare, the creator of the psychopathy checklist (PCL-R).

It consists of 20 questions, each scoring between zero and two, with a maximum score of 40.

Snowden said most people scored below five, while 25 or over was typically the threshold for psychopathy.

Anderson scored himself about an eight or a nine.

"Psychopathy is on a dimension that I could place you, I could place myself," Snowden said.

"They can be very strong and, in some ways, make good leaders... but there are many deficits to their leadership and it's all about them and not about other people," he added;

"The fundamental trait of psychopathy is that lack of empathy for other people.

"Most psychopaths never kill anybody. But they may take advantage of other people, exploit other people, not care about other people."

Snowden said some corporate environments may appeal to people with psychopathic traits as they often need "to be quite unemphatic" and focused on making money.

There is no treatment available for psychopathy, as "psychopaths often believe that there's nothing wrong with them".

Anderson was recently evaluated by Kerry Daynes, a consultant and forensic psychologist, who concluded he was not a psychopath.

Daynes said he may have become a "situational psychopath", adapting his behaviour to thrive in an environment that rewarded ruthless ambition.

She added: "You don't need to be a psychopath to thrive - for a while at least - in a psychopathic culture."

She said Anderson was able to "crank up" his "darker personality characteristics" to succeed in his environment, something that was in "the sweet spot that most people can't attain".

Despite rapidly rising through the ranks of London finance, Anderson said he became disillusioned by "greed, reckless risk-taking and rule breaking in the industry".

"I just looked around and thought 'I'm on the wrong team'... What on Earth are you doing? You are part of the problem."

He left and became the anonymous columnist City Boy, for the London Paper every Friday, revealing a world of excessive wining, dining, drugs and illicit sex.

It transformed into a the book Cityboy that sold more than 400,000 copies and was translated into six languages.

He's also recently just published his fifth book which explores how adopting psychopathic traits can help people climb the corporate ladder.

Anderson said he was a "less pleasant person" while in the corporate world but hopes he is a "warmer person" now

"I'm more able to feel like trying to have integrity and not manipulate and be ruthless."

Although, he joked, his wife may disagree about him not having any of his psychopathic traits left.

articles.title: 'Another tax bombshell?' and 'Terror plot targets'
articles.summary: Several of today's papers feature Andy Burnham's latest plans as PM, including experts warning of a potential tax rise to help cover his social care plan.
articles.body:
The co-pilot who attempted to take control of a flight travelling to Israel had previously advocated for violence against women while studying remotely at a UK university, according to the Sunday Telegraph. , During his time with Buckinghamshire New University, Hamam al-Hammami allegedly said women should be "stomped on" and slapped. The university had its licence to sponsor international students suspended on the day of the attack. Both the Home Office and the institution said the incidents were unrelated.

The Sunday Mirror leads on the court appearance of two Iranian men charged with plotting terror attacks on the Jewish community in Manchester. Its front page features pictures of the alleged targets, which include a synagogue and museum.

The Sunday Times says a leaked document suggests Russia has introduced strict rules on fighting-aged men, to get them to sign up for the military. A letter shared with the paper suggests men aged between 18 and 30 now must present their draft papers before they can take out a mortgage, buy and sell property, or be recorded as a business owner.

The Mail on Sunday focuses on Home Office figures showing taxpayers have funded more than 1,000 free hijabs this year for migrants arriving in the UK illegally. A Home Office spokesman told the paper it had a legal duty to provide basic clothing, including cultural and religious items.

The Sun on Sunday leads on comments by the footballer Andy Carroll , who says he was sexually assaulted by a former cast member of the BBC show, Fame Academy. The dance coach, Kevin Adams, was convicted in 2023 and jailed for 20 months. The paper's front page features images of the two men.

A report in the Sunday Telegraph says a church in Hampshire is appealing for the public's help in decoding a recently-discovered labyrinth . The single, winding path designed for walking meditation and prayer was hidden by an altar table at St Mary's Church in Itchen Stoke. A member of the Churches Conservation Trust is quoted as saying it feels like being in the Da Vinci Code.

And turkey is off the menu for Christmas lunch at the King's Highgrove Estate, according to the Sunday Express. It says the traditional bird will be replaced by chicken for the festive lunches, with all proceeds going to charity. Brussels sprouts also no longer feature, in an attempt to cut costs.

articles.title: Urna eletrônica: a história da criação do sistema de votação | G1
articles.standfirst: Ideia surgiu em uma conversa entre o então presidente do TSE e um técnico de informática; projeto reuniu engenheiros e pesquisadores de instituições de São José dos Campos e deu origem à urna usada nas eleições brasileiras.
articles.summary: A urna eletrônica nasceu de uma conversa informal e do trabalho de engenheiros de São José dos Campos para modernizar as eleições no Brasil.
articles.body:
O ano era 1995. Em Brasília, uma conversa durante uma partida de tênis ajudou a dar início a uma das maiores transformações das eleições brasileiras.

O então presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), ministro Carlos Velloso, conversava com o técnico em informática Paulo Camarão sobre a possibilidade de informatizar a votação no país.

A ideia rapidamente deixou a quadra e foi parar no TSE. Para transformar o projeto em realidade, a Justiça Eleitoral reuniu especialistas de diferentes áreas. Entre eles, um grupo de engenheiros e técnicos que ficou conhecido como os “ninjas”.

A equipe ficou responsável por transformar as ideias iniciais em um projeto de hardware e software e estabelecer os requisitos para a nova máquina. Em dezembro de 1995, o TSE publicou o edital para a produção dos equipamentos e, em março de 1996, a empresa brasileira Unisys venceu a licitação.

Poucos meses depois, a urna eletrônica estreou nas eleições municipais de 1996 . Cerca de 30% do eleitorado votou pelo novo sistema naquele primeiro pleito. A implantação foi ampliada gradualmente e, hoje, a tecnologia é utilizada em todos os municípios brasileiros.

O grupo de "ninjas" era coordenado por Paulo Camarão e reunia profissionais como Paulo Nakaya, Mauro Hashioka, Antônio Ésio Salgado, o “Toné”, Oswaldo Catsumi e Giuseppe Janino.

Também participaram representantes de instituições e órgãos ligados à tecnologia e à defesa, entre eles o Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (Inpe).

Parte dessa história passa por São José dos Campos , onde estavam instituições como o Inpe, o Instituto Tecnológico de Aeronáutica (ITA), o então Centro Técnico Aeroespacial (CTA) e o Instituto de Estudos Avançados (IEAv).

Segundo o TRE-SP, o grupo técnico se reunia duas vezes por semana, no TSE ou no próprio TRE-SP, para apresentar os trabalhos e trocar conhecimentos sobre o projeto.

Foto 1: Urna usada em 1996. Foto 2: Ministro Carlos Velloso testa urna. Foto 3: Comissão técnica que ficou conhecida como 'os ninjas' — Foto: TRE/SP/Arquivo

A mudança proposta pelo TSE tinha dois grandes objetivos: reduzir problemas e possibilidades de fraude relacionados à votação e à apuração manual e acelerar a divulgação dos resultados.

Antes da urna eletrônica, os eleitores votavam em cédulas de papel. Depois do encerramento da votação, os votos precisavam ser contados manualmente. O processo podia levar dias e envolvia uma grande operação de conferência e contabilização dos votos.

Com a urna eletrônica, o registro dos votos passou a ser feito digitalmente e a apuração pôde ser concluída em poucas horas depois do fechamento das seções eleitorais.

Para o cientista político José Maurício Cardoso do Rego, a mudança também ajudou a reduzir mecanismos tradicionais de fraude ligados à contagem manual. “Com a implantação das urnas eletrônicas, há uma inibição clara desse processo de fraude”, afirmou.

Urna eletrônica usada nas eleições municipais no ano de 1996. — Foto: TRE-SP

A primeira versão, a UE96, tinha apenas 2 megabytes de memória e utilizava disquetes para armazenamento e transferência de dados. Nas eleições de 1996, cerca de 30% do eleitorado votou eletronicamente.

A implantação foi ampliada gradualmente e hoje a urna é utilizada em todos os municípios brasileiros.

Em 30 anos, o equipamento passou por diversas atualizações. Atualmente, conta com mecanismos como assinaturas digitais, criptografia e sistemas de verificação desenvolvidos pela Justiça Eleitoral.

O TSE também realiza o Teste Público de Segurança (TPS), no qual especialistas são convidados a tentar identificar vulnerabilidades nos sistemas eleitorais.

Infográfico: Veja a cronologia da urna eletrônica no Brasil — Foto: Arte/g1

Da tecnologia dos anos 1990 aos equipamentos atuais

Em três décadas, a urna eletrônica passou por diversas mudanças. Os equipamentos atuais contam com recursos de segurança que não existiam nos primeiros modelos, incluindo assinaturas digitais, criptografia e mecanismos próprios de verificação desenvolvidos pela Justiça Eleitoral.

A segurança também é submetida a testes antes das eleições. O Tribunal Superior Eleitoral realiza periodicamente o Teste Público de Segurança (TPS), que reúne especialistas para tentar identificar vulnerabilidades nos sistemas e equipamentos utilizados no processo eleitoral.

A lógica é colocar os mecanismos de proteção à prova antes que eles sejam utilizados pelos eleitores. Segundo os profissionais que participaram da criação da urna, a preocupação com a segurança já existia desde os primeiros protótipos.

A participação de São José dos Campos nessa história está ligada ao próprio perfil tecnológico da cidade. Instituições como Inpe, ITA, CTA e IEAv concentravam pesquisadores e engenheiros envolvidos em projetos de alta complexidade.

Esse conhecimento acabou sendo incorporado ao desenvolvimento da urna eletrônica, em uma colaboração entre diferentes áreas e instituições. A história da urna, portanto, também é parte da história tecnológica do Vale do Paraíba.

Em 2026, a urna eletrônica completa três décadas de uso oficial no Brasil. Nesse período, a tecnologia deixou de ser uma novidade e passou a fazer parte da rotina das eleições brasileiras.

A experiência brasileira também ultrapassou as fronteiras do país. Segundo dados citados pelos pesquisadores envolvidos no projeto, ao menos 33 países já utilizaram algum modelo de votação eletrônica inspirado ou relacionado à experiência brasileira.

articles.title: Cachorro perdido inspira criação de rede social para pets no PI | G1
articles.standfirst: Lançada no Dia Mundial dos Animais, plataforma gratuita permite divulgação de pets desaparecidos, encontrados e para adoção, além de interação entre tutores.
articles.summary: Lançada no Dia Mundial dos Animais, plataforma gratuita permite divulgação de pets desaparecidos, encontrados e para adoção, além de interação entre tutores.
articles.body:
Empresário cria rede social para reunir pets desaparecidos, encontrados e para adoção no Piauí — Foto: Reprodução/Arquivo Pessoal

O desaparecimento de um cachorro levou o empresário Wanderson Oliveira a transformar uma experiência pessoal em uma iniciativa para ajudar outros tutores. Ele criou uma rede social voltada para pets, em que é possível divulgar animais desaparecidos, encontrados e disponíveis para adoção.

O SeePets é lançado neste domingo (4), data em que é celebrado o Dia Mundial dos Animais.

Natural de José de Freitas , no Centro-Norte do Piauí, Wanderson relembrou que ainda era estudante de Ciência da Computação quando, em 2016, aguardava um ônibus e percebeu um cachorro aparentemente perdido em uma avenida de Teresina .

"Fiquei incomodado, pois não podia fazer nada. No outro dia, vi um cartaz oferecendo recompensa para quem encontrasse o mesmo cachorrinho. Desde então, fiquei pensando em um aplicativo que pudesse notificar sobre pets perdidos ou encontrados nas proximidades do local onde o animal desapareceu ou foi localizado", relembrou o empresário.

O empresário afirmou ao g1 que, na época, não possuía conhecimento técnico suficiente nem recursos financeiros para desenvolver o projeto.

Foi apenas em abril de 2026 que Wanderson conseguiu tirar a ideia do papel e desenvolver a ferramenta. Para isso, contou com o suporte dos amigos Samuel Pinheiro e Raphael Moraes.

Segundo ele, a proposta da plataforma é centralizar informações sobre os animais em um único ambiente e utilizar recursos de localização para ampliar as chances de reencontro .

"Quando um animal desaparece, é encontrado ou precisa de adoção, as informações geralmente ficam espalhadas entre grupos de WhatsApp, perfis de redes sociais e publicações que rapidamente perdem alcance", afirmou

No aplicativo, os tutores também podem cadastrar os próprios animais , criar perfis , publicar fotos e vídeos , e interagir com outros usuários , como em uma rede social tradicional.

Wanderson destacou ainda que a plataforma permite visualizar ocorrências em um mapa , gerar cartazes automaticamente e reunir informações que facilitem a busca por animais .

"A plataforma pretende estimular a participação comunitária, a adoção responsável, a conscientização sobre bem-estar animal e a colaboração entre tutores e pessoas dispostas a ajudar", contou

Segundo o empresário, o aplicativo é totalmente gratuito para tutores . No futuro, funcionalidades pagas deverão ser disponibilizadas para empresas e profissionais do setor pet.

"É emocionante ver esse sonho sair do papel depois de tanto tempo. A minha expectativa é que o cumpra seu papel, conectando pessoas e pets fazendo finais felizes com seus tutores", relatou emocionado.

*Vitória Bacelar, estagiária sob supervisão de Ilanna Serena.

articles.title: 'Senti até o cheiro', disse motorista de app que devolveu R$ 19 mil | G1
articles.standfirst: Valor pertencia a um empresário e caiu por uma fresta no câmbio do caminhão em Descalvado (SP), na segunda (28). Busca nas redes ajudou na localização.
articles.summary: Valor pertencia a um empresário e caiu por uma fresta no câmbio do caminhão em Descalvado (SP), na segunda (28). Busca nas redes ajudou na localização.
articles.body:
'Senti até o cheiro, era dinheiro mesmo', disse o motorista de aplicativo Clóvis Sanches, de 62 anos, que encontrou R$ 19 mil em dinheiro caídos no asfalto no bairro Morada do Sol, em Descalvado (SP), e devolveu aos donos.

Clóvis havia acabado de desembarcar um passageiro e ajudá-lo com as compras quando percebeu o maço de notas na rua e decidiu devolver tudo aos donos, que fizeram um apelo nas redes sociais.

O motorista contou que ajudou um passageiro a descarregar uma compra e não havia nada caído no local. "Naquele momento não tinha nada ali. Na hora que eu saí, eu olhei para lá e falei: 'Olha, é um negócio estranho, é um pacote. Vou chegar lá perto para ver'".

"Dinheiro! Eu falei: 'Não é possível, isso é gozação'. Eu olhei assim, senti até o cheiro, era dinheiro mesmo", lembrou Clóvis.

O valor pertencia ao empresário Gabriel Umbelino Gomes. Ele tinha acabado de retornar de uma viagem de trabalho em Minas Gerais, onde recebeu a quantia em espécie pelo serviço prestado.

O dinheiro seria utilizado para honrar compromissos e pagar os custos de outra obra que ele está desmanchando.

Motorista de aplicativo encontra R$ 19 mil na rua e devolve aos donos no interior de SP — Foto: Renan Ciconelo/EPTV

Ao retornar a Descalvado, Gabriel passou em uma loja de autopeças no Centro da cidade para fazer um pagamento e seguiu para casa. O empresário guardou o restante do valor em uma sacola plástica colocada no assoalho do caminhão , bem ao lado do câmbio.

O que ele não percebeu é que o veículo estava com uma abertura no vão do câmbio. A sacola deslizou, passou pelo buraco e despencou no asfalto — a menos de 200 metros da entrada da residência do casal.

Motorista de aplicativo encontra R$ 19 mil na rua e devolve aos donos no interior de SP — Foto: EPTV/Reprodução

Gabriel só deu falta do montante quando estacionou o caminhão na porta de casa. Diante do sumiço, a família começou uma verdadeira corrida contra o tempo atrás de imagens de câmeras de segurança, acreditando que o dinheiro tivesse caído na região central da cidade.

A esposa de Gabriel, a administradora Ana Paula Bradieri Gomes, relatou que o desespero deu lugar ao desânimo conforme as horas passavam.

"Até terça-feira a gente ainda tinha esperança, porque a gente foi atrás de câmera, achando que tinha caído no centro. Mas passou terça e nós já não acreditávamos mais não. Eu já tinha falado para ele: 'Minha vida, bora trabalhar, correr atrás'", contou Ana Paula.

A reviravolta na história aconteceu após Ana Paula fazer um apelo e publicar o ocorrido nas redes sociais. A postagem circulou pela cidade até chegar ao conhecimento de Clóvis , que manteve o montante guardado e intacto aguardando a identificação dos donos.

Quando se encontraram, na quarta (30), o motorista fez questão de entregar tudo.

"Podia ter devolvido só um pouco para não pesar tanta consciência, mas não. Chegamos lá, o valor estava todo lá, não pensou duas vezes. Ele me entregou o dinheiro e falou que foi criado honesto e que o que não é dele ele não queria. A gente é muito grato, porque poderia muito bem ter posto no bolso e fingido que nada tinha acontecido", disse a administradora.

Administradora agradece motorista por devolver R$ 19 mil em Descalvado (SP) — Foto: Renan Ciconelo/EPTV

articles.title: Britain restored a catchment where water voles disappeared; 20 ponds, 26,000 trees and 15 hectares of wildflowers later, they are returning
articles.summary: Water voles are being reintroduced to North Devon more than 25 years after being declared functionally extinct in the area in 2000.
articles.body: Water voles are being reintroduced to North Devon more than 25 years after being declared functionally extinct in the area in 2000. The National Trust, which announced the news on 29 June 2026, has carried out a major restoration project across the Combesgate catchment at Woolacombe since 2022. The work included creating 20 ponds and scrapes, planting 26,000 trees and sowing 15 hectares of wildflower seed. About 110 voles have been released so far. Paul South of the National Trust called the return "an important moment for nature in North Devon", delivered with the North Devon Coast National Landscape.Habitat restoration work helped water voles return to WoolacombeThe Trust said the reintroduction follows a major habitat restoration project at Woolacombe. According to the official press release by the National Trust, extensive work has been carried out across the Combesgate catchment since 2022 to restore habitats and natural processes in local waterways. The BBC reported that the aim was to create the right conditions for the animals' return.The Trust listed the work as follows: creating 20 ponds and scrapes, removing land drains, planting 26,000 trees and sowing 15 hectares of wildflower seed. Natural flood management measures and rewetting were also introduced along 1,700 metres of watercourse, alongside conservation grazing to support biodiversity. The press release said this forms part of a wider programme across North Devon to restore a more natural, wetter landscape that is better able to cope with the impacts of climate change. It added that the changes are helping to reconnect habitats and slow the flow of water through the landscape.How are water voles being reintroducedThe National Trust said the reintroduction has been carefully managed with Derek Gow Consultancy, whose expertise has helped deliver a planned programme to give the animals the best chance of survival. According to the press release, the voles are first placed in protective pens on site, where they are monitored and cared for before gradually dispersing into the surrounding habitat. According to the BBC, the animals leave the pens in their own time, which helps to reduce stress. Trail cameras have been set up to capture them as they begin to explore their new environment.Paul South told the BBC that about 110 voles have been released so far and that this number might be topped up depending on how they are doing. He said he would expect the population to more than double, perhaps triple, by the end of the season, before numbers drop back again at the end of winter. According to the BBC, he added that if the voles do well, they will expand outwards, and a few neighbouring watercourses are being watched to see whether they turn up there.How do water voles support other wildlifeThe National Trust said water voles' burrows create flowering habitats that support bugs, butterflies and other riverside species. South told the BBC the burrows also provide dens for other animals and create a more complex habitat. He said the voles are prey for animals such as herons and foxes, and that they breed a lot and so can cope with this. In the press release, he described the return as "an important moment for nature in North Devon", saying it shows wildlife can recover with the right conditions.The project was delivered in partnership with North Devon Coast National Landscape, with funding support from Farming in Protected Landscapes. The Trust relies on volunteers to monitor watercourses in the area, and South asked local people to get in touch to watch for burrows and mink, and to report both to mammal societies. Hannah Ford, the Trust's Fundraising Manager, invited supporters to donate to the Adopt a Plot initiative in North Devon, which the press release said supports habitat restoration and the reintroduction of native species such as pine martens, red squirrels and water voles. Under its ten-year strategy, the Trust aims to work with partners to create 250,000 hectares of nature-rich landscapes, an area it described as one-and-a-half times the size of Greater London.You use AI every day. articles.title: OpenAI's Sam Altman criticises Anthropic’s push to explore AI consciousness and religion
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has criticised efforts to give artificial intelligence a religious or spiritual dimension, in what appeared to be a pointed response
articles.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has criticised efforts to give artificial intelligence a religious or spiritual dimension, in what appeared to be a pointed response to work being explored by rival AI company Anthropic.Altman said he was "very uncomfortable" with attempts to give AI models religious significance or treat them as entities that could replace human judgement. His comments come as Anthropic researchers are exploring questions around whether AI systems could one day be conscious and how religious ideas might shape the way such systems behave.Altman raises safety concerns"I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue," Altman said in a post to X.The comments were widely seen as a criticism of Anthropic and its co-founder Dario Amodei, who previously worked with Altman at OpenAI.The disagreement is about more than whether AI can think. It concerns whether future AI systems could have consciousness, feelings or some form of moral status, and whether humans should treat them differently if they do.Anthropic explores AI and religionThe debate intensified after The New York Times reported that Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah had been speaking with religious leaders about AI consciousness and the possibility of building stronger moral behaviour into AI models.According to the report, Olah had also explored whether AI models could use practices inspired by religion. One idea considered was whether an AI system could take part in something similar to Catholic confession, allowing it to acknowledge mistakes and potentially influence its future behaviour.Before a Vatican event in May, Olah also reportedly tried to persuade advisers to Pope Leo to take the possibility of conscious AI systems more seriously.The issue has now become a wider debate within the technology industry, with some prominent AI researchers openly questioning whether AI models should be given any kind of moral or spiritual standing.Scientists push backGoogle DeepMind principal research scientist Jon Barron criticised the idea in a post on X."I am disturbed by how some of my fellow AI researchers keep trying to elevate the moral standing of checkpoints and harnesses," Barron wrote. "I hope the rest of us on Team Meatbag reject this movement and stay focused on solving real problems and helping actual humans."The discussion has also drawn attention from Pope Leo, who has been vocal about the risks AI poses to human creativity. On Friday, he urged the Catholic Church to work with artists to protect human creativity, saying, "Algorithms lack the spark of humanity."The growing disagreement comes as AI safety discussions have traditionally focused on more immediate risks such as cyberattacks and the use of AI to assist in developing biological weapons.But the latest debate raises a more fundamental question about the future of AI. If machines ever become conscious, should humans treat them as more than tools, and could religion have a role in deciding how they should behave?Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic immediately responded to requests for comment on Altman's post.You use AI every day. Demonstrators chanted slogans including "We have the keys of all the city" and carried banners such as "There won't be peace for rentism."Housing vote defeat fuels protestsThe protests followed the rejection of two government-backed housing decrees in Congress on Friday. The measures included suspending evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, extending rental leases, increasing taxes on tourist apartments and restricting purchases of residential properties by investment funds.The first decree was defeated 178-172, while the second was rejected 184-166. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's minority coalition does not have a parliamentary majority and failed to secure enough support from smaller regional parties.The defeat has also fuelled speculation that Sánchez could call an early general election, although elections are not due until next summer.The latest wave of protests was triggered by the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Kerala home minister Ramesh Chennithala has ordered a Vigilance investigation into allegations of irregularities involving Chief Election
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Kerala home minister Ramesh Chennithala has ordered a Vigilance investigation into allegations of irregularities involving Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar during his tenure as the state’s Public Works Department Secretary in 2006, news agency ANI reported.The case concerns the death by suicide of Malaysian civil engineer Lee See Been, who was associated with the PATI-BEL consortium involved in the upgradation of MC Road under the Kerala State Transport Project. Been’s suicide note reportedly mentioned Gyanesh Kumar.The investigation has been ordered following allegations that external pressure was exerted and that the original inquiry into the case was derailed.Chennithala has directly instructed the Vigilance Director to conduct a thorough inquiry into the allegations of external influence in the case involving Gyanesh Kumar and take appropriate action based on the findings, the Home Minister’s Office said."Yesterday, Malayinkeezhu Venugopal, a Congress activist, gave me a petition regarding the malpractices and corrupt activities of Gyanesh Kumar when he was PWD secretary in Keralam... The representation reveals some of the serious issues. Also, in between, my Malaysian project engineer, Lee, committed suicide. In the suicide note, it has been mentioned about PWD Secretary Gyanesh Kumar very clearly. So the government cannot sit idle. I cannot become a mute spectator... I had forwarded it to the vigilance director to go into the details of the petition and take legal action to deliver justice," Chennithala said.Official sources said the Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) will conduct a probe into the allegations, as cited by news agency PTI.The development comes as opposition parties, student organisations and youth groups held protests in Delhi and Mumbai on Friday, demanding Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and claims of mass voter deletions.Around 700 people were detained in Delhi, while thousands gathered at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park despite police denying permission for the demonstrations.In Delhi, those detained included AAP leaders Atishi, Saurabh Bharadwaj and Sanjeev Jha, AISA president Neha Bora, CPI(M) leaders M A Baby and Brinda Karat, CPI national secretary P Sandosh Kumar, RJD leader Manoj Jha, social activist Yogendra Yadav, DYFI president A A Rahim and former JNUSU president Aishe Ghosh.The agitation intensified after media reports claimed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections on at least 14 occasions over 10 months regarding decisions and procedures linked to the SIR exercise and other electoral matters.The reported objections covered issues including voter deletions, Form 6 and access to electoral-roll databases. articles.title: Burnham scraps controversial plans to curb jury trials
articles.summary: The key policy idea announced by David Lammy when he was justice secretary will no longer go ahead.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has scrapped controversial plans to curb some jury trials.

Sir Keir Starmer's government had introduced proposals to allow judges to make the sole decision on cases that would lead to a sentence of less than three years.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said only complex fraud and financial offences would be judge-alone - and it proposes that thousands of medium-level crimes should stay with volunteer magistrates, who sit without a jury.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said he had changed course after hearing the "strength of feeling" about the original proposals.

Criminal lawyers have welcomed the decision and the Conservatives say it is a "major victory" for those who fought to defend trial by jury.

Former Justice Secretary David Lammy first announced the plans in December following a recommendation in a major review of the court system in England and Wales.

The series of radical reforms, including scaling back jury trials, were presented as the best way of turning around record backlogs which, in turn, were exacerbating the prison population crisis.

The backlog - which has led to record delays for defendants and victims - currently stands at nearly 81,000 cases - having rocketed largely thanks to cuts before the pandemic and court closures during the national lockdowns. Official projections have estimated it could reach 100,000 before the next general election and, in a worst case scenario, climb to double that number by 2035.

There are, however, indications the backlog is now stabilising after the government committed unlimited funding to pay for more judges to sit in courts that were otherwise being unused.

Under the original plans, Lammy had wanted to reserve jury trials for the most serious "indictable" offences - meaning cases that are always sent to Crown Court, including murder and rape.

Less serious offences, where the sentence would be no more than three years, would be decided without a jury in the Crown Court by a judge alone. Even less serious offences would stay in magistrates' courts, abolishing defendants' right to ask for a trial by jury when they feel that is their best chance of beig cleared.

The proposals triggered an outcry across many parts of the criminal justice world, with many opponents saying that eroding the 800-year-old right to trial by jury would not solve the backlogs.

Norris said that he remained committed to bringing down the backlog and delivering swifter justice.

But he added: "I have heard the strength of feeling on the proposals for increasing the number of judge-alone trials in the Crown Court and have made the decision to change course.

"This allows us to start that work far earlier, ensuring that under this government we do not have victims waiting endlessly for justice.

"Justice delayed is justice denied, and I am committed to maximising efficiencies in our system alongside record investment. I remain committed to structural reform which is crucial if we are to bring down the backlog."

Andrew Thomas KC - chairman of the Criminal Bar Association, which represents barristers who work in crown and magistrates courts - said the profession was "delighted".

"Justice needs juries," he said. "Nothing inspires more public trust than 12 ordinary citizens from all walks of life deciding the facts of a case together.

"We are also pleased that the government is going ahead with important changes in the bill to protect victims and witnesses at trial. These include new powers to prevent unfair questioning about a complainant's behaviour and to support witnesses to give their best evidence."

But Thomas warned that plans to keep more middle-ranking cases before magistrates by abolishing defendants' rights to ask for a jury trial could backfire - not least because of a shortage of magistrates.

"The proposal to strip defendants of their right to elect a crown court trial, combined with doubling magistrates' sentencing powers to two years, would shift 25,000 cases a year - including 5,500 jury trials - out of the crown court," he said.

"These are not minor offences. It includes serious and sensitive cases including assaults, sexual assaults, child abuse and grievous bodily harm. Our volunteer magistrates do an excellent job but they are completely unequipped to try complex, multi-day trials.

"It would be a car crash if they tried to do it, especially at this time."

Barrister Karl Turner, a Labour MP who was suspended from the parliamentary party after he criticised the government's plans to reform jury trials, thanked Burnham "for his support during my campaign".

Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said: "This is a major victory for everyone who fought to defend trial by jury, and Conservatives led that fight from day one. Labour have been forced to abandon its central attack on jury trials in the Crown Court."

Court backlog will continue to rise even with new reforms, Lammy says

articles.title: Trump leaks senator’s number after row over clock-change bill: What’s the dispute
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has publicly clashed with fellow Republican Senator Tom Cotton over a proposal to keep daylight saving time in place throughout
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has publicly clashed with fellow Republican Senator Tom Cotton over a proposal to keep daylight saving time in place throughout the year.The dispute took an unusual turn on Saturday when Trump posted what he said was Cotton’s cellphone number on social media and asked people in Arkansas to call the senator and pressure him to support the proposal.The move came after Trump accused Cotton of holding up the Sunshine Protection Act, a bill that would stop Americans from changing their clocks twice a year.What is Trump proposingUnder the current system, Americans move their clocks one hour forward in March and one hour back in November.Moving the clock forward means sunrise and sunset appear one hour later on the clock. For example, if the sun would normally rise at 7 am and set at 6 pm, the clock change would make them appear as 8 am and 7 pm. This gives people more daylight in the evening.Trump wants the March setting to remain in place throughout the year. That means Americans would not move their clocks back in November.Trump has repeatedly criticised the twice-yearly clock change, calling it “ridiculous”. On Saturday, he said the practice “discombobulates everybody.”The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House of Representatives in July by 308 votes to 117 but has remained stalled in the Senate.Why is Cotton opposing itCotton, who represents Arkansas, says keeping daylight saving time throughout the year would make winter mornings too dark.He pointed to an earlier attempt to adopt permanent daylight saving time in the US. The country tried it in 1974, but public support quickly fell as people complained about late sunrises during winter. The change was abandoned in less than a year.“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” Mr. Cotton said in a social media post. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark.”Cotton's position puts him at odds with Trump despite the two Republicans generally being political allies.Trump asks voters to call CottonTrump included a letter from PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp in his post supporting the bill. Rolapp argued that an extra hour of daylight in the evening could allow Americans to play 23 million additional rounds of golf each year.Trump urged people in Arkansas to contact Cotton directly.“To the Great People of Arkansas, please let your Senator know it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN for the United States Senate,” Mr. Trump said. “Call Tom on his cellphone.”Two officials confirmed that the number Trump posted belonged to Cotton. His office did not respond to a request for comment. Calls to the number went to an automated message saying the recipient was “temporarily unavailable.”Cotton later defended his position without directly referring to Trump's post. Trump responded within an hour, accusing Cotton of blocking the bill and asking why he was doing so, other than “ego?”Why does the issue matterThe debate is not simply about whether Americans prefer longer evenings. Many sleep scientists favour the existing system because morning sunlight helps keep people's body clocks aligned with the natural day.The 1974 experiment is also central to the argument. Supporters of permanent daylight saving time say the extra evening light would benefit activities such as sports and leisure, while opponents warn that winter mornings could become significantly darker. Trump has previously used a similar tactic against another senator.During the 2016 Republican presidential primary, he publicly displayed the phone number of Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, who was then competing against him for the Republican nomination, and encouraged people to call him.At Graham's funeral in July, Trump acknowledged that sharing the number was something he “shouldn’t have done.”“And I remember the number,” Mr. Trump said, reciting the digits again at the funeral. “If anybody wants to give it a shot,” he added.You use AI every day. articles.title: Beavers beat humans to restoring a closed Massachusetts golf course, building a 6-to-8-foot dam before crews arrived
articles.summary: When a Massachusetts golf course closes, the land does not stay quiet for long.
articles.body: When a Massachusetts golf course closes, the land does not stay quiet for long. At the former Pine Grove Golf Course in Northampton, beavers moved in roughly a year before restoration crews, damming a small stream with a wall of mud and sticks six to eight feet tall. According to WAMC Northeast Public Radio, the new pond is already drawing wood ducks and swallows back to the site. Meanwhile, the city and state ecologists are ripping up pavement and reshaping the brook, in what project partners call a flagship example of golf course rewilding, a model for other retired courses.How the Pine Grove golf course drained the landGolf courses have been closing across the Northeast, and especially in Massachusetts. WAMC cites a Boston Business Journal estimate that at least 57 courses closed in the state between 2012 and 2022. Northampton acquired Pine Grove in 2020. The course once had 18 holes, a clubhouse, and a small pond, and Sarah LaValley of the city's Office of Planning and Sustainability told the station the owner had hoped for years that another golf group would take over before the city stepped in.Tom Lautzenheiser, a senior conservation ecologist with the Massachusetts Audubon Society, explained to WAMC why the green fairways were not good for the environment. Because golfers want dry ground, water was channelled through cisterns and trench drains and sent straight to Nashawannuck Brook, then downstream toward the Arcadia wildlife sanctuary. In a watershed of roughly 300 acres, about 100 acres were golf course, and Lautzenheiser said the grass behaved like pavement.The beaver dam that arrived before the machinesKate Bentsen, an ecological restoration specialist with the state Division of Ecological Restoration, told WAMC that human work was only getting underway while the local beavers had started their own restoration at least a year earlier. She described a very small stream that has been flooded by a large dam, which began developing about a year ago and stands somewhere between six and eight feet tall, impounding a considerable area.The results are visible. Bentsen said birds are returning, including wood ducks and swallows. According to the WAMC report, the wall of mud and sticks is close to impenetrable, yet a healthy stream still flows through its base, keeping water in the habitat during mild drought conditions.What human crews are doing along the brookThe human work is large too. WAMC reports that heavy machinery has spent at least a month tearing up the road along Old Wilson Way between Rocky Hill and Florence roads, which LaValley described as the city's first ecologically related road closure. Travis Sumner of SumCo Eco-Contracting said phase one has already removed over 800 feet of pavement and will restore 1,600 feet of the stream by taking out the rock-lined channel that rushes water off the site, with much of the work hoped to be finished by the end of June. The public was asked to stay out until July 1.Phase two, according to LaValley, includes removing a man-made dam at a nearby irrigation pond, which is not the beaver dam, plus more wetland and trail work. Planners also hope to build an accessible loop called the All Persons Trail, with a bridge over a culvert that has failed. Tom Annese, a land planning assistant for Northampton, told WAMC that the open character of the site is rare among the city's mostly wooded, hilly conservation land, and that its wet conditions made housing mostly impractical.Funding, trails, and a model for other coursesRecent work was funded in part by the state division and the city, totalling at least $720,000. Later construction could cost as much as $3 million, and LaValley said she is optimistic about winning more state grants while acknowledging that plans may need rethinking if the money does not come through.Project partners see wider significance. Julianne Busa of the engineering and design firm Fuss & O'Neill told WAMC that Pine Grove is the first project of its kind in Massachusetts and that the state division hopes it will serve as a flagship for rewilding retired courses. Similar efforts are following, she said, including a driving range being rewilded in Stow and the Beaver Brook project in Williamsburg and Northampton.That second project belongs to The Trustees, the Massachusetts conservation organisation, which acquired the Beaver Brook Golf Course in July 2025. The Trustees also says it is learning from regional golf course restoration projects, naming Pine Grove and its Nashawannuck Brook work among them.David Eisenhauer of the state division told WAMC that the work is not so much creating something new as returning something that was always there, a connection between people and nature.You use AI every day. articles.title: A family foundation began restoring 250 acres of overworked Ohio farmland in 1989; it is now a wildlife reserve with Walden Pond
articles.summary: At first glance, Thoreau Wildlife Reserve looks less like a former farm and more like a patchwork of Ohio landscapes.
articles.body: At first glance, Thoreau Wildlife Reserve looks less like a former farm and more like a patchwork of Ohio landscapes. Meadows give way to woodland, wetlands sit alongside prairie, and older sections of forest provide another layer of habitat. Across roughly 250 acres, two miles of walking trails now lead visitors through these different settings. Yet the land did not begin this way. In 1989, the Diehl Family Foundation began a long restoration effort on farmland that had been heavily worked. More than 30 years later, the property includes a pond created by a dam, planted woodland and areas allowed to develop into more natural habitats. The reserve opened to the public in 2020.The Diehl family’s 1989 project reshaped 250 acres of Ohio farmlandThe transformation began in 1989, when the Diehl Family Foundation started a programme intended to change the character of the 250-acre property. The farmland had been heavily used, so the first stage involved preparing the soil for a different kind of landscape.According to Thoreau Wildlife Reserve, that autumn, work began on the ground itself. The following year, a dam was constructed to hold water and create what is now known as Walden Pond. A meadow was seeded, prairie was established and the first trees for a pine plantation went into the soil.The changes were not completed in a single planting season. The project continued for years as the landowners, family members, local workers and volunteers carried out further work across the property.A man-made pond became part of the landscapeWalden Pond is one of the clearest examples of how the reserve's present landscape was deliberately created. The water body was formed after the dam was built as part of the early restoration work. Around it, the character of the property gradually became more varied. Wetlands, prairie, hardwood woodland and areas of old growth forest now occupy parts of the reserve. Rather than replacing the farmland with one uniform type of planting, the long-running project resulted in several distinct habitats across the site.The changes also created space for a range of plants and wildlife. The reserve sits among a landscape still dominated in part by farmland, making the restored property a contrasting area of habitat.The 250-acre reserve opens its restored habitats to visitorsVisitors can now explore the reserve on four nature trails covering about two miles. The routes pass through meadows, woodlands, wetlands and old growth forest, giving the property several different settings within the same 250-acre site. The reserve has also been used for educational purposes. Students and faculty from Defiance College have carried out ecology studies on the property over the years, adding an academic use to the land alongside its role as a wildlife habitat.Signs placed along the trails also feature thoughts associated with H.D. Thoreau, whose ideas and writing inspired the name of the reserve.Bird nesting becomes part of the reserve’s restoration workThe restoration effort has extended beyond trees and vegetation. Thoreau Wildlife Reserve works with the Audubon Sanctuary Program to encourage several bird species to nest on the property, including bluebirds, wood ducks and mallard ducks.The different habitats provide a mixture of conditions across the reserve. Wet areas, woodland and open spaces each form part of the wider landscape, while the continued management of the property is intended to support wildlife living and nesting there.The reserve opened to visitors in 2020Although the land had been undergoing changes for decades, public access came much later. In 2020, after years of preparation, Thoreau Wildlife Reserve opened its trails to visitors. The stated purpose was to make the property available for education, recreation and appreciation of the natural environment while maintaining its role as a refuge for plants and wildlife. Opening the land also marked a new stage in a project that had begun with soil preparation and planting more than 30 years earlier.Today, access remains fairly controlled. The reserve is open from dawn until dusk, with parking available but limited. Visitors are required to remain on the designated trails, and only walking is permitted within the preserve. Dogs can be brought in, but they must remain on a lead.A decades-long transformation created today’s wildlife reserveVisitors are asked to follow leave-no-trace principles and respect the site's natural resources. The restrictions are part of how the reserve manages public access while keeping the restored habitats intact. The property is located at 10485 Haller Road and covers approximately 250 acres. What began in 1989 as an effort to change the condition and use of heavily worked farmland has since developed into a mixture of planted and naturally developing habitats, centred partly around the man-made Walden Pond.The landscape is therefore the product of a long process rather than a single restoration project. Fields were prepared, water was held behind a new dam, trees and prairie were planted, and subsequent decades of work gradually changed the character of the property. By the time the public arrived in 2020, the site had become a wildlife reserve with trails running through several distinct ecosystems.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court has taken suo motu cognisance of the proposed relocation of Delhi's 135-year-old Central Secretariat Library, which holds more than 8.5 lakh books.The court's intervention comes amid reports that the library, currently located in Shastri Bhawan, has not been allotted space in the new Central Vista Plan. Reports said the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs and the Central Public Works Department were still looking for suitable space for the library.The proposed relocation has also raised concerns about ensuring proper facilities for the preservation of its extensive collection.Government says space has been providedThe Union ministry of housing and urban affairs, however, has rejected reports that the library has been left without space under the redevelopment plans."Contrary to a few reports, it is clarified that space for the Central Secretariat Library has been provided for in the Kartavya Path redevelopment plan. articles.title: Portland is covering ordinary traffic signal boxes with colourful artwork, but it is not just for decoration
articles.summary: Portland is giving ordinary traffic signal boxes a colourful new purpose, covering the metal cabinets with artwork that does more than brighten street
articles.body: Portland is giving ordinary traffic signal boxes a colourful new purpose, covering the metal cabinets with artwork that does more than brighten street corners. The city is using durable vinyl wraps to make these pieces of essential infrastructure more attractive while testing whether the coverings can also discourage graffiti and reduce the need for repeated repainting. The approach has already produced dozens of designs across Portland, from roses and clouds to animals and comic-style images, turning objects that once faded in the background into small pieces of public art.Why Portland is covering traffic signal boxes with colourful artworkThe project centres on traffic signal boxes and utility cabinets that contain electrical equipment used to operate traffic lights, pedestrian crossings and other traffic functions. They are often positioned at busy intersections, along narrow pavements and beside places where people wait for public transport or spend time on foot.According to Axios, Portland’s Public Environment Management Office began wrapping utility boxes with graffiti-resistant vinyl coverings in 2025. The office was created during the pandemic to address visible quality-of-life issues such as graffiti, rubbish and neglected public spaces. The signal-wrap project was developed as one way of dealing with both the appearance and maintenance of these highly visible boxes.The change is noticeable because many of the boxes had previously been repeatedly tagged and then painted over. Those repairs could leave mismatched patches of paint across the metal surfaces. The new coverings provide a consistent design instead of another layer of plain paint.The artwork also has a practical purposeThe colourful designs are not simply being added to make intersections look better. The vinyl is intended to resist graffiti, giving the city an opportunity to see whether a more durable surface can reduce the amount of cleaning and repainting required over time.Axios reported that Portland had 130 wrapped signal boxes, with nearly 50 more in development, and more than a dozen designs in use. The average installation cost was about $1,750. The city is continuing to monitor the wraps to determine whether they can provide a financial benefit by reducing long-term maintenance work.The designs themselves vary widely. Some feature oversized roses, clouds and comic-book-style graphics, while others include animals, cartoon characters and lumberjack imagery. There are also Portland Trail Blazers-themed designs, giving some of the otherwise ordinary street equipment a connection to the city’s sporting culture.Portland has tested the idea through community artThe current effort builds on an idea that has appeared in Portland communities before. In 2016, the Portland Bureau of Transportation supported a pilot project in East Portland that used a traffic signal box as a small public artwork.A Portland Bureau of Transportation news advisory from November 2016 said residents and local stakeholders had expressed a strong desire for public art during discussions about the future of the Division Midway business district. The Division Midway Alliance researched low-cost approaches and developed the ‘Art on the Box’ concept, which was intended both to beautify the area and deter graffiti.The first installation was placed at Southeast 122nd Avenue and Division Street. The Portland Bureau of Transportation described it as the city’s first use of a traffic signal box for low-cost public art. Its four panels represented the seasons and local culture, including the cultural diversity of the Division Midway area.Student artists helped turn one box into a local landmarkEast Portland News reported that the earlier project involved students from David Douglas High School’s main and Fir Ridge campuses, working under the direction of an adult art coordinator. Their designs were created at school and transferred digitally to a durable vinyl wrap.The resulting artwork replaced a formerly grey electrical utility box with a collection of student-created images. The material, commonly used on vehicles such as trucks and buses, provided a practical surface for the artwork while allowing the box to continue serving its original purpose. The project also showed how a relatively small object could provide an accessible place for young artists to contribute to their neighbourhood.One Portland neighbourhood has linked the art with its surroundingsA more recent example can be found at Peace Memorial Park in Portland’s Lloyd neighbourhood. According to Lloyd EcoDistrict, the organisation worked with local artist Irene Ramirez and the city to wrap a utility box near one of Portland’s busiest cycling areas.The artwork focuses on local pollinators and includes the name of Peace Memorial Park. The box had previously been blank and covered in graffiti. The new design was intended to give the location a stronger sense of place while offering cyclists, pedestrians and visitors something colourful to notice as they passed.The Lloyd EcoDistrict also tested the wrap shortly after installation. During a community clean-up, a small amount of graffiti that had appeared on the artwork was removed with an eco-friendly cleaner. The organisation said the graffiti-resistant vinyl could be maintained with a simple wipe-down rather than requiring the whole surface to be repainted.Portland is making small infrastructure part of the streetscapeThe idea has also been used in Portland, Maine, showing that utility boxes can serve as small public canvases in more than one city with the same name. A 2016 report from News Center Maine described a project in which local artists painted utility boxes around downtown Portland to make otherwise plain infrastructure more attractive. The city said the effort was intended to beautify the urban landscape, encourage civic participation and support local artists.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: A 20-year-old US Marine stationed in Japan’s Okinawa prefecture was arrested on Sunday on suspicion of robbing and murdering a local woman.Davin Ballard, stationed at the US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, is suspected of killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi and taking her wallet and backpack at a hotel in Naha in the early hours of Saturday, according to Okinawa prefectural police.Police said Ballard was seen entering the hotel with Yagi, who was found dead there on Saturday morning. The Marine has denied the allegations.Ballard was later spotted walking alone in Naha’s entertainment district on Saturday night, where a police officer questioned and detained him, according to police.The alleged involvement of a US serviceman prompted Japan’s foreign ministry to lodge a protest with US ambassador to Japan, George Glass, on Sunday.Vice foreign minister Takehiro Funakoshi raised the case with Glass, who told him that the US side would fully cooperate with the investigation and take all possible measures to prevent a recurrence, the ministry said.Glass separately said on X that he had spoken to Okinawa governor Genta Koja, offering condolences and pledging full US cooperation as the investigation continued.Japanese police said they would investigate the case in cooperation with the US military.Serious offences including murder, rape and robbery have previously fuelled tensions between local communities and the large US military presence in the Okinawa prefecture.Local police have stated that they have handled more than 100 criminal cases involving US service members and related personnel in 2025.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bridges under attack: Why Russia is targeting Kyiv's vital crossings
articles.summary: Russia has stepped up attacks on key bridges across the Dnipro River in Kyiv, disrupting major transport links in the Ukrainian capital and raising
articles.body: Russia has stepped up attacks on key bridges across the Dnipro River in Kyiv, disrupting major transport links in the Ukrainian capital and raising questions over Moscow’s wider strategy of targeting the city’s critical infrastructure.According to the BBC, Russia has targeted major bridges in Kyiv in recent days, with Moscow claiming that the crossings are being used to move Ukrainian troops and military equipment. The strikes come amid a broader Russian campaign against Ukrainian infrastructure, as Moscow intensifies attacks on targets across the country.The southern bridge was struck repeatedly on October 1 and 2, while the northern bridge was hit on October 3, according to Reuters. The attacks damaged parts of the bridges and forced restrictions on traffic, adding to severe congestion across Kyiv.The bridges are critical because they connect Kyiv's eastern and western banks across the Dnipro River. More than one-third of the capital's roughly three million residents live on the eastern bank, while around 500,000 people cross the river every day for work, according to Reuters.Why are these bridges so important?The Dnipro effectively divides Kyiv, making these crossings essential for the city's daily functioning.The bridges importance goes beyond ordinary road traffic because the crossings carry road, public transport and, in the case of the Southern Bridge, metro traffic. Reuters reported that the Southern Bridge is one of the city's main routes connecting the two sides of Kyiv.The bridges also have potential military significance. Russia has specifically claimed that Ukrainian troops and military cargo are transported across the crossings. That makes the bridges valuable not only as civilian transport arteries but also as potential logistics routes for Ukrainian forces.A Ukrainian aviation expert cited by the Kyiv Independent said the weapons used in the strikes appeared more suited to disrupting traffic than bringing down the massive bridge structures.What impact are the strikes having?The immediate impact has been major disruption to movement across Kyiv. After the Southern Bridge was struck, traffic was suspended and authorities introduced restrictions on other crossings, contributing to severe congestion on alternative routes.Reuters reported that the disruption was particularly significant because the eastern bank of Kyiv relies heavily on the bridges for connections with the rest of the capital.The strikes have also affected public transport. Damage to the Southern Bridge disrupted metro services, while the strike on the Northern Bridge damaged trolleybus infrastructure.Kyiv's authorities have had to consider alternative arrangements to maintain movement across the river, including the possibility of pontoon crossings if damage to the bridges persists.Repeated closures could slow the movement of people, disrupt supply routes and put additional pressure on a city already facing attacks on other critical infrastructure. Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia's broader campaign is aimed at making life increasingly difficult in major Ukrainian cities.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
